questions.question: What are the dimensions of the coefficient of viscosity $\eta$?

solution.key_concept: Newton's law of viscosity, $F = \eta A\, dv/dx$
steps: Rearrange the law: $\eta = \dfrac{F}{A\,(dv/dx)}$.
The dimensions of $F$ are $[MLT^{-2}]$ and those of $A$ are $[L^2]$.
The velocity gradient $dv/dx$ has dimensions $[T^{-1}]$.
solution.why_not_others: $[MLT^{-1}]$ is the dimension of momentum. $[ML^{-1}T^{-2}]$ is the dimension of pressure. $[MT^{-2}]$ is the dimension of surface tension.
solution.common_trap: Forgetting that the velocity gradient has dimensions $[T^{-1}]$. Dropping it gives the dimension of pressure.
solution.time_saving_tip: Remember that the SI unit of $\eta$ is Pa s. Multiplying $[ML^{-1}T^{-2}]$ by $[T]$ gives the answer directly.

questions.question: Eight identical small rain droplets each fall with a terminal velocity of $5\ \text{cm s}^{-1}$ through air. They coalesce to form a single spherical drop. What is the terminal velocity of the new drop?

solution.key_concept: Terminal velocity $v_t \propto r^2$. When $n$ drops merge, the volume is conserved.
steps: Volume conservation gives $\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3 = 8 \times \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$, so $R = 2r$.
Since $v_t \propto r^2$, $v_t' = v_t (R/r)^2 = 4 v_t$.
Equivalently, $v_t' = n^{2/3} v_t = 8^{2/3} \times 5 = 20\ \text{cm s}^{-1}$.
solution.why_not_others: $10\ \text{cm s}^{-1}$ uses $v \propto r$. $40\ \text{cm s}^{-1}$ multiplies by $n$. $80\ \text{cm s}^{-1}$ wrongly assumes $v \propto r^4$.
solution.common_trap: Multiplying the terminal velocity by the number of drops instead of by $n^{2/3}$.

questions.question: A metal ball of radius $1\ \text{mm}$ and density $5800\ \text{kg m}^{-3}$ falls through a liquid of density $1300\ \text{kg m}^{-3}$. The viscosity of the liquid is $10$ poise. Find the terminal velocity of the ball. Take $g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.

solution.key_concept: $v_t = \dfrac{2r^2(\sigma-\rho)g}{9\eta}$, with $\eta$ in Pa s
steps: Convert the viscosity: $\eta = 10$ poise $= 1\ \text{Pa s}$.
Find the density difference: $\sigma - \rho = 5800 - 1300 = 4500\ \text{kg m}^{-3}$.
Substitute: $v_t = \dfrac{2 \times (10^{-3})^2 \times 4500 \times 10}{9 \times 1} = \dfrac{0.09}{9} = 0.01\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.
solution.why_not_others: $1.29\ \text{cm s}^{-1}$ ignores buoyancy and uses $\sigma$ alone. $0.1\ \text{cm s}^{-1}$ wrongly takes 10 poise as $10\ \text{Pa s}$. $1.58\ \text{cm s}^{-1}$ adds the two densities instead of subtracting them.
solution.common_trap: Forgetting the buoyancy factor $(\sigma - \rho)$, or not converting poise to Pa s.
solution.time_saving_tip: Note that 1 Pa s = 10 poise, so 10 poise is simply 1 Pa s.

questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: A small steel ball and a larger steel ball, released in the same viscous oil, finally fall with the same terminal velocity.
statements.R: The terminal velocity of a sphere falling through a viscous fluid is proportional to the square of its radius.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: $v_t = \dfrac{2r^2(\sigma-\rho)g}{9\eta}$, so $v_t \propto r^2$
steps: Both balls have the same $\sigma$, and they fall through the same $\rho$ and $\eta$.
Since $v_t \propto r^2$, the larger ball has a larger terminal velocity.
So A is false and R is true.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): A is false but R is true
solution.why_not_others: A contradicts the $r^2$ dependence, so every option that treats A as true is wrong.
solution.common_trap: Carrying over the free-fall idea that all bodies fall alike. That holds only in the absence of viscous drag.

questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: When a sphere falling through a viscous liquid attains its terminal velocity, the viscous drag on it equals its weight.
statements.II: For spheres of the same radius falling in a given liquid, a graph of terminal velocity against $\sigma/\rho$ is a straight line with zero terminal velocity at $\sigma/\rho = 1$.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: At terminal velocity, weight = buoyancy + viscous drag. Also, $v_t \propto (\sigma - \rho)$.
steps: At terminal velocity the net force is zero, so the drag equals weight minus buoyancy, not the full weight. Statement I is incorrect.
Write $v_t = \dfrac{2r^2\rho g}{9\eta}\left(\dfrac{\sigma}{\rho} - 1\right)$. This is linear in $\sigma/\rho$ and zero at $\sigma/\rho = 1$. Statement II is correct.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
solution.why_not_others: Statement I ignores the buoyant force, so any option calling it correct fails. Statement II follows directly from the formula.
solution.common_trap: Forgetting buoyancy in the force balance at terminal velocity.

questions.question: Which of the following is true for streamline flow of a fluid?
options: The velocity of the fluid at a given point changes continuously with time
The velocity of the fluid at a given point does not change with time
Two streamlines can cross each other at a point
The flow is irregular and contains eddies

solution.key_concept: Definition of streamline (laminar) flow
steps: In streamline flow, the velocity at any given point stays constant in time.
Streamlines never cross. Eddies are a feature of turbulent flow.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): The velocity of the fluid at a given point does not change with time
solution.why_not_others: A time-varying velocity and eddies describe turbulent flow. Crossing streamlines would mean two velocities at one point, which is impossible.
solution.common_trap: Confusing 'velocity constant at a point' with 'velocity the same everywhere'. The speed can still differ from point to point.

questions.question: Water flows steadily through a horizontal pipe whose diameter reduces from $4\ \text{cm}$ to $2\ \text{cm}$. The speed of water in the wider part is $0.5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. What is its speed in the narrower part?

solution.key_concept: Equation of continuity: $A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$, with $A \propto D^2$
steps: Rearrange: $v_2 = v_1 (D_1/D_2)^2$.
Substitute: $v_2 = 0.5 \times (4/2)^2 = 0.5 \times 4 = 2.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.
solution.why_not_others: $1.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ uses the diameter ratio instead of the area ratio. $0.125\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ inverts the ratio. $8.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ uses the fourth power of the diameter ratio.
solution.common_trap: Using the ratio of diameters rather than the ratio of areas.
solution.time_saving_tip: Halving the diameter quarters the area, so the speed becomes four times as large.

questions.question: Water (density $1000\ \text{kg m}^{-3}$, viscosity $1.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{Pa s}$) flows at $0.2\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ through a pipe of diameter $2\ \text{cm}$. Find the Reynolds number and the nature of the flow.

solution.key_concept: $R_e = \rho v D/\eta$. $R_e > 2000$ indicates turbulent flow.
steps: Substitute: $R_e = \dfrac{1000 \times 0.2 \times 0.02}{1.0 \times 10^{-3}} = \dfrac{4}{10^{-3}} = 4000$.
Since $4000 > 2000$, the flow is turbulent.
solution.why_not_others: $400$ comes from using the wrong viscosity value. $4000$ with streamline flow misreads the criterion. $2000$ comes from using the radius instead of the diameter.
solution.common_trap: Substituting the radius in place of the diameter $D$.

questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_II.label: II
list_II.text: Conservation of mass for an incompressible fluid

list_II.label: III
list_II.text: Ratio of inertial force to viscous force

list_II.label: IV
list_II.text: Speed beyond which the flow becomes turbulent

solution.key_concept: Basic definitions for fluid flow
steps: The Reynolds number is the ratio of inertial force to viscous force: A-III.
Critical velocity is the speed at which turbulence sets in: B-IV.
The equation of continuity expresses mass conservation, $Av = $ constant: C-II.
Crowded streamlines indicate higher speed: D-I.
solution.why_not_others: Every other option swaps at least one definition, such as the Reynolds number with critical velocity, or continuity with crowded streamlines.
solution.common_trap: Mixing up the Reynolds number, which is dimensionless, with critical velocity, which is a speed.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about streamline and turbulent flow are correct?

statements.A: The critical velocity is higher for a more viscous liquid.
statements.B: For a given liquid, the critical velocity is higher in a wider pipe.
statements.C: The Reynolds number is a dimensionless quantity.
statements.D: In steady incompressible flow through a tube of varying cross-section, the volume flow rate is the same at every section.
statements.E: A denser fluid has a higher critical velocity, other factors being the same.

options: A, B, C and D only

solution.key_concept: $v_c = R_e \eta/(\rho D)$; continuity gives $Q = Av = $ constant
steps: Since $v_c \propto \eta$, statement A is true.
Since $v_c \propto 1/D$, a wider pipe has a lower critical velocity, so B is false.
$R_e$ is a ratio of forces, so it is dimensionless and C is true.
$Q$ is constant along the tube, so D is true.
Since $v_c \propto 1/\rho$, E is false.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): A, C and D only
solution.why_not_others: Options containing B or E include false statements. 'A and C only' leaves out the true statement D.
solution.common_trap: Assuming that a denser fluid or a wider pipe resists turbulence. Both actually lower the critical velocity.
solution.time_saving_tip: Write $v_c \propto \eta/(\rho D)$ once and read off A, B and E from it.

questions.question: A small hole is made in the side of an open water tank, $5\ \text{m}$ below the free surface. Find the speed of efflux of water from the hole. Take $g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.

solution.key_concept: Torricelli's law: $v = \sqrt{2gh}$
steps: Substitute: $v = \sqrt{2 \times 10 \times 5} = \sqrt{100}$.
solution.why_not_others: $100\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ forgets the square root. $7.1\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ uses $\sqrt{gh}$. $5.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ uses $\sqrt{gh/2}$.
solution.common_trap: Dropping the factor of 2 in $\sqrt{2gh}$.
solution.time_saving_tip: The efflux speed equals the speed of free fall from height $h$.

questions.question: A tank stands on level ground and is filled with water to a height of $2.5\ \text{m}$. A small hole is made in its side wall, $0.5\ \text{m}$ below the water surface. How far from the base of the tank does the jet strike the ground?

solution.key_concept: Range of the jet: $R = 2\sqrt{h(H-h)}$
steps: The depth is $h = 0.5\ \text{m}$, so the hole is at height $H - h = 2.0\ \text{m}$ above the ground.
Substitute: $R = 2\sqrt{0.5 \times 2.0} = 2\sqrt{1} = 2.0\ \text{m}$.
solution.why_not_others: $1.0\ \text{m}$ drops the factor of 2. $2.24\ \text{m}$ uses $H$ in place of $H-h$. $2.5\ \text{m}$ is the maximum range, which occurs only for a hole at $H/2$.
solution.common_trap: Using the total height $H$ instead of the height of the hole above the ground.

questions.question: Water flows steadily through a horizontal pipe. The cross-section reduces from $10\ \text{cm}^2$ to $5\ \text{cm}^2$, and the speed in the wider section is $1\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Find the pressure difference between the wide and narrow sections. Take the density of water as $1000\ \text{kg m}^{-3}$.

solution.key_concept: Continuity plus Bernoulli: $\Delta P = \frac{1}{2}\rho(v_2^2 - v_1^2)$
steps: From continuity, $v_2 = v_1 A_1/A_2 = 1 \times 10/5 = 2\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.
Then $\Delta P = \frac{1}{2} \times 1000 \times (4 - 1) = 1500\ \text{Pa}$.
solution.why_not_others: $500\ \text{Pa}$ uses $(v_2 - v_1)^2$. $3000\ \text{Pa}$ omits the factor $\frac{1}{2}$. $2000\ \text{Pa}$ uses $\frac{1}{2}\rho v_2^2$ alone.
solution.common_trap: Squaring the difference of the speeds instead of taking the difference of their squares.

questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: In steady streamline flow through a horizontal pipe, the pressure at a narrow section is greater than at a wide section.
statements.R: In steady streamline flow through a horizontal pipe, the fluid moves faster where the cross-section is smaller.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: Continuity combined with Bernoulli for a horizontal pipe
steps: Continuity gives a higher speed at a smaller area, so R is true.
For a horizontal pipe, Bernoulli gives $P + \frac{1}{2}\rho v^2 = $ constant, so a higher speed means a lower pressure.
The pressure is therefore lower at the narrow section, and A is false.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): A is false but R is true
solution.why_not_others: A reverses the pressure-speed relation, so every option that treats A as true is wrong.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that a squeezed fluid must be at higher pressure.

questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: Each term in Bernoulli's equation, $P + \frac{1}{2}\rho v^2 + \rho g h$, has the dimensions of pressure, i.e. energy per unit volume.
statements.II: For a tank filled with liquid to a height $H$, a hole at depth $H/4$ gives a larger horizontal range of the jet than a hole at depth $H/2$.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: Dimensions of the Bernoulli terms; range $R = 2\sqrt{h(H-h)}$ is maximum at $h = H/2$
steps: Every term of Bernoulli's equation has the dimension of pressure, which equals energy per unit volume. Statement I is correct.
At $h = H/4$: $R = 2\sqrt{\frac{H}{4}\cdot\frac{3H}{4}} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}H \approx 0.87H$.
At $h = H/2$: $R = H$, which is the maximum. Statement II is incorrect.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
solution.why_not_others: Statement II contradicts the result that the range is maximum at $h = H/2$.
solution.common_trap: Believing that a hole nearer the top always gives the longest jet.
solution.time_saving_tip: The range is maximum at $h = H/2$, so any other depth gives a shorter range.

questions.question: Which of the following units is equivalent to the SI unit of surface tension?

solution.key_concept: Surface tension equals the force per unit length, which also equals the surface energy per unit area.
steps: Write $S = F/l$, with unit $\text{N m}^{-1}$.
Multiplying numerator and denominator by m gives $\text{N m}/\text{m}^2 = \text{J m}^{-2}$.
solution.why_not_others: $\text{N m}^{-2}$ is the unit of pressure. $\text{J m}^{-1}$ is a newton, the unit of force. $\text{N m}$ is the unit of energy or torque.
solution.common_trap: Confusing surface tension with pressure.

questions.question: A soap film on a wire frame has surface tension $0.03\ \text{N m}^{-1}$. Its area is increased isothermally from $10\ \text{cm}^2$ to $40\ \text{cm}^2$. Find the work done.

solution.key_concept: For a film with two surfaces, $W = 2S\Delta A$
steps: The change in area is $\Delta A = 30\ \text{cm}^2 = 3 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^2$.
Then $W = 2 \times 0.03 \times 3 \times 10^{-3} = 1.8 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{J}$.
solution.why_not_others: $9.0 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{J}$ counts only one surface. $2.4 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{J}$ uses the final area instead of the change in area. $3.6 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{J}$ uses $4S$.
solution.common_trap: Forgetting that a soap film has two surfaces.

questions.question: A light straight wire of length $5\ \text{cm}$ rests on a horizontal rectangular frame and is pulled by the soap film formed between them. The surface tension of the soap solution is $0.04\ \text{N m}^{-1}$. What force is needed to hold the wire in equilibrium?

solution.key_concept: $S = F/l$; a film pulls with both of its surfaces, so $F = 2Sl$
steps: The wire is pulled by both surfaces of the film, so $F = 2Sl$.
Substitute: $F = 2 \times 0.04 \times 0.05 = 4.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{N}$.
solution.why_not_others: $2.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{N}$ counts only one surface. $8.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{N}$ counts four surfaces. $0.40\ \text{N}$ leaves the length in cm.
solution.common_trap: Using $F = Sl$ for a film instead of $F = 2Sl$.

questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_II.label: III
list_II.text: Decreases both surface tension and angle of contact

solution.key_concept: Angle of contact and the effect of impurities on surface tension
steps: Water on glass has $\theta \approx 0^\circ$: A-IV.
Mercury on glass has $\theta \approx 140^\circ$: B-II.
Detergents decrease both $S$ and $\theta$: C-III.
Highly soluble NaCl increases $S$: D-I.
solution.why_not_others: The other options swap the water and mercury contact angles, or swap the effects of detergent and NaCl.
solution.common_trap: Assuming that every impurity lowers surface tension. Highly soluble salts raise it.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about surface tension and angle of contact are correct?

statements.A: The surface tension of a liquid increases as its surface area is increased.
statements.B: The surface tension of a liquid becomes zero at its critical temperature.
statements.C: The angle of contact is measured inside the liquid, between the solid surface and the tangent to the liquid surface.
statements.D: Small liquid drops are spherical because a sphere has the minimum surface area for a given volume.
statements.E: When cohesion exceeds adhesion, the angle of contact is acute.

solution.key_concept: Properties of surface tension and the angle of contact
steps: Surface tension is independent of the surface area, so A is false.
Surface tension falls with temperature and vanishes at the critical temperature, so B is true.
C is the definition of the angle of contact, so it is true.
D is true because a sphere minimises surface area for a given volume.
When cohesion dominates, $\theta$ is obtuse, as for mercury on glass, so E is false.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): B, C and D only
solution.why_not_others: Options containing A or E include false statements. 'B and D only' leaves out the true statement C.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that stretching a surface changes its surface tension. Stretching only adds surface energy in proportion to the added area.
